BOUNDING CAVEAT, from CAPRI's own report: it states production impacts are likely OVERESTIMATED because co-benefits are not modelled, and that magnitudes 'should not be taken as definitive in absolute terms'. So CAPRI's -15% is itself an upper bound, which narrows the apparent gap further. This is a magnitude check, not ground truth.

nitrogen_balance_unit_bugs.note: Setting out to re-express the nitrogen instrument on a SURPLUS basis (so CAPRI's tiered GNB rule from JRC121368 could be applied) instead uncovered that our gross nitrogen balance was meaningless. Measured before using it: median surplus -170196 kg N/ha, against a real EU gross nitrogen balance of ~45-50. Two independent unit errors. BUG 1 - GRAS FRESH MATTER. The crop N uptake term is area x yield x N-content-per-tonne, but GRAS yield is FRESH MATTER in kg/ha (~36000) while every other crop is t/ha. Grass therefore supplied 10.13m of a 10.20m total N uptake in FR10 - 99.3% - and drove the balance hugely negative, with a nitrogen-use efficiency of 107. This is the SAME fresh-matter artifact that previously corrupted the fertiliser module and the income module; it is the third module it has been found in. Fixed by converting GRAS to a dry-matter tonnage basis (fresh kg/ha -> t/ha, ~20% DM) rather than dropping it, since grass N does leave the field via grazing livestock. BUG 2 - MANURE N EFFECTIVELY ZERO. Organic N was computed as heads*1000 * kgN/head / 1e6, dividing by a further 1000 relative to every other term (deposition is area in 1000 ha x 20 kg/ha). Activity levels are already in 1000 head and _n_excretion returns kg N/head (DCOW 105.3, matching the literature 100-120), so the product is already in the right unit. FR10 showed 0.0 kg N/ha of organic input against a real EU average near 55. RESULT: median N surplus -170196 -> +54 kg N/ha across 30 regions (real EU ~45-50). FR10 components now all credible: mineral 133.6, organic 6.8, fixation 5.0, deposition 20.0, uptake 119.8, SURPLUS 43.8 kg N/ha. Pinned by test_nitrogen_balance_is_physically_plausible, which checks both the aggregate and that manure N is non-zero. CONSEQUENCE FOR EARLIER WORK: any environmental result that used n_surplus was affected. The GHG and MACC results do NOT depend on it (they run off enteric/manure CH4 and N2O emission factors, not the balance), so the EcAMPA validation stands. But the nitrogen balance itself should not have been described as validated, and the README claim that N excretion matches CAPRI MANN within ~12% covers excretion, not the balance. STILL OPEN: with a credible surplus in hand, CAPRI's tiered GNB rule (25% cut on the first 50 kg/ha, 50% for 50-100, 75% for 100-150, 100% above 150) can now be applied on the correct basis - which was the original objective and is the next step.

nutrient_surplus_instrument.status: implemented on the correct basis; three of four F2F targets now comparable
nutrient_surplus_instrument.note: Implemented CAPRI's Farm-to-Fork nutrient target as JRC121368 specifies it, after the nitrogen-balance unit bugs were fixed (without which the surplus basis did not exist). THE RULE: a TIERED reduction of the gross nitrogen balance - 25% on the first 50 kg N/ha of surplus, 50% on 50-100, 75% on 100-150, 100% above 150. Implemented as SupplyModel.tiered_surplus_target(), resolved PER REGION inside the solve because the target depends on each region's own surplus. Exposed as PolicyScenario.nutrient_surplus_target. THE TRANSLATION, and the trap in it: the solve constrains APPLIED nitrogen while CAPRI's target acts on SURPLUS, and the two differ by roughly a factor of four here (median surplus 54 kg N/ha against applied intensity 241). A surplus cut has to come out of inputs, so the applied-N ceiling falls by the same ABSOLUTE amount as the required surplus cut, NOT the same proportional amount - applying a 27% surplus cut as a 27% cut in applied N would have been about four times too aggressive. This is exactly the mismatch that caused the instrument to be EXCLUDED from the earlier comparison rather than forced. APPLIED TO OUR REGIONS: median surplus 54 kg N/ha, median target 40, median implied cut 27% - e.g. DE11 76 -> 50 (34% cut), applied-N ceiling 241 -> 215. The instrument alone gives cereals -2.6%, oilseeds -0.6%, mean activity change 1.84%. COMPARISON AGAINST PUBLISHED CAPRI (JRC121368), three representable instruments together (landscape 10% + organic 25% + nutrient surplus), 40 regions: cereals -13.1% against CAPRI's -15%; oilseeds -7.9% against -15%; permanent/fruit&veg -1.0% against -12%. READING IT: cereals is now close, and sensibly below CAPRI given we omit the pesticide target (which CAPRI applies with a 10% yield loss across cereals, oilseeds, vegetables and permanents). Oilseeds at roughly half of CAPRI's figure is a plausible partial-bundle result. PERMANENT CROPS REMAIN THE OUTLIER at -1.0% against -12%, and this is now the clearest candidate for a real defect rather than a missing-instrument artefact: CAPRI's pesticide yield loss hits permanents directly and organic conversion hits horticulture hard, but a 12-point gap is large even so. Worth a targeted investigation. BOUNDING CAVEAT: JRC121368 states its own production impacts are likely OVERESTIMATED because co-benefits are not modelled, and that magnitudes 'should not be taken as definitive in absolute terms', so CAPRI's figures are an upper bound.

permanent_crop_response_gap.status: diagnosed - a data-coverage gap, not a code defect
permanent_crop_response_gap.note: Investigated the one large divergence left in the published-CAPRI comparison: permanent crops and fruit/veg move -1.0% in CAPRI-mod against JRC121368's -12%. RULED OUT FIRST: (a) the organic instrument DOES reach permanent crops - all eight are in CROPS and in the activity set; (b) the margin hit is UNIFORM, every crop losing 6-8% net revenue under a 25% organic target (ES61: SWHE -7.3%, OLIV -6.3%, CITR -7.4%, TOMA -5.9%), so permanents are not being skipped; (c) the permanent-land bound is an UPPER limit, so it cannot stop crops shrinking. ROOT CAUSE - ELASTICITY COVERAGE. Realized own-price elasticities: SWHE +1.012, BARL +0.972, RAPE +0.694, but OLIV +0.090, WINE +0.100, OFRU +0.120, CITR +0.120, TOMA +0.308, OVEG +0.334. Permanent crops are roughly TEN TIMES less responsive than cereals, so a 6-7% margin cut moves them ~1% - exactly the observed result. WHY: CAPRI's PELA file (pmp_own_price_elasticities.csv) contains NO permanent crops. SWHE (217 regions), BARL (223) and RAPE (155) are present and our realized values track them closely (1.01 vs CAPRI 1.05; 0.97 vs 1.21). OLIV, OFRU, CITR, WINE, OVEG and TOMA are ABSENT, so all 248 regions fall back to LITERATURE_DEFAULT (verified in the provenance table: 248/248 LITERATURE_DEFAULT for every permanent crop, against 165/248 REGIONAL_CAPRI for SWHE). The defaults are low by construction - OLIV and WINE 0.10, OVEG 0.18, TOMA 0.20. SO THE MODEL IS BEHAVING CORRECTLY GIVEN ITS INPUTS. The -1% is the honest consequence of assuming permanent crops are near-inelastic, which is a defensible agronomic prior (orchards and olive groves take years to establish or grub up) but is NOT what CAPRI assumes in its Green Deal run, where permanents fall 12%. TWO CANDIDATE EXPLANATIONS FOR THE REMAINING GAP, not yet separated: (1) CAPRI's pesticide target applies a 10% yield loss directly to permanent crops - an instrument we cannot represent at all, and a yield shock bypasses the elasticity question entirely; (2) our permanent-crop elasticities may simply be too low relative to CAPRI's, which cannot be checked from the PELA file because it carries no permanent crops. TO RESOLVE: extract CAPRI's own permanent-crop supply elasticities (they exist inside CAPRI's supply model even though they are absent from this PELA export) and compare. Until then the honest statement is that permanent-crop response is governed by literature priors rather than CAPRI-derived values, and should not be presented as CAPRI-consistent.
permanent_crop_response_gap.capri_elasticity_source_traced: TRACED where CAPRI's own supply elasticities live, so the permanent-crop gap can be closed. They are NOT in the PELA export we have (pmp_own_price_elasticities.csv carries only annual crops - SWHE 217 regions, BARL 223, RAPE 155, and no OLIV/OFRU/CITR/WINE/OVEG/TOMA at all). THE SYMBOL: p_elasSupp(region, XX, YY, 'CAL') - the calibrated supply elasticity matrix used by CAPRI's supply model. supply/calibrate_supply.gms:508-509 fills it from p_netPutElas, and it is the quantity our PELA file is a partial export of. THE FILE: cgemrk/map_data.gms:269 loads it explicitly - results\arm\elas_%NTSLVL%_%BAS%%SIM%%inputDataId%%NTM%.gdx, containing p_elasSupp alongside p_hessNQSupp, p_hessNQFeed, p_hessNQDairy, p_hessNQProc, p_pdGL and p_pbGL. arm/trim_elas.gms:32 reads the same family as elas%BAS%%SIM%%reg_agg%%modId%%inputDataId%%NTM%.gdx, and capmod/to_esim.gms:61 loads p_ElasSupp from results\arm\elas%bas%%cur%. So a file named elas*.gdx should exist under results\arm\ in any installation that has run the market module. ORIGIN: arm/trim_elas.gms shows the underlying values come from WATSIM (p_elasSuppOri), trimmed and calibrated by CAPRI. WHAT TO EXTRACT: gdxdump <results\arm\elas*.gdx> symb=p_elasSupp, then take the diagonal (XX == YY) entries for OLIV, OFRU, CITR, WINE, OVEG and TOMA. Cross-check on arrival: the annual crops in the same file should reproduce the PELA values we already have (SWHE ~1.05, BARL ~1.21), which confirms the right symbol and basis before the permanent-crop numbers are used. IF OBTAINED: this would replace literature priors (OLIV/WINE 0.10, OVEG 0.18) with CAPRI-derived values for the whole permanent-crop group, and would separate the two competing explanations for the -1.0% vs -12% gap - our elasticities being too low, versus the missing pesticide yield shock.

permanent_crop_elasticity_fix.status: SUPERSEDED - the earlier rescaling was WRONG; corrected from CAPRI calibrated data
permanent_crop_elasticity_fix.note: The user supplied p_elasSupp.txt, a gdxdump they had already made of CAPRI's supply elasticity matrix (73530 lines, cross-price included). Extracted the diagonal: 2635 own-price entries, 80 regions, 45 crops. WHAT THE FILE IS, and the cross-check that failed: it is the MARKET-model supply elasticity at MEMBER-STATE and world-region level (codes include AT000000 but also AFR_LDC, ARG), with market commodities (WHEA, TWIN) rather than PMP activities (SWHE, WINE). The cross-check against our PELA values did NOT reproduce - BARL reads 0.395 here against PELA's regional 1.21 - so the ABSOLUTE levels are not transferable: these are national market elasticities, ours are regional PMP calibration targets. Using the levels directly would have been wrong. WHAT IS ROBUST, and is the finding: the RELATIVE structure. In CAPRI's own data, permanent crops and vegetables have a median own-price elasticity of 0.970 against 0.392 for annual crops - i.e. permanents are 2.47x MORE elastic than annuals. Our literature priors had them at 0.08-0.15 against 0.20-0.40 for annuals, i.e. ~10x LESS elastic. The relative ordering was INVERTED, by roughly 25x. The prior was defensible in isolation (orchards and groves are slow to establish or grub up) but is not what CAPRI assumes. FIX: permanent-crop and vegetable defaults rescaled to CAPRI's relative structure while staying on our own annual-crop scale - annuals average ~0.26 here, so permanents are set to ~2.47x that (OLIV 0.62, WINE/APPL/CITR/TAGR/TOMA 0.64, OFRU 0.63, OVEG 0.61). VALIDATION: base fidelity IMPROVED slightly (11.33%% -> 11.28%% on annual crops), olive base fidelity stays essentially exact (0.06%% -> 0.32%%), and 248/248 regions still converge - so the change did not destabilise PMP calibration. EFFECT ON THE GREEN DEAL COMPARISON: permanent/fruit&veg response moves from -1.0%% to -4.5%% against CAPRI's published -12%%, a 4.5x increase in the right direction, while cereals (-13.1%% vs -15%%) and oilseeds (-7.9%% vs -15%%) are unchanged. The residual gap is consistent with the pesticide instrument we cannot represent, which CAPRI applies as a 10%% yield loss falling directly on permanent crops. Pinned by test_permanent_crops_are_not_pathologically_inelastic.

pesticide_instrument.status: implemented as a BRACKET; CAPRI sits inside it for all three aggregates
pesticide_instrument.note: The pesticide target had been recorded as blocked on PLAP cost data. Re-reading CAPRI's own implementation (JRC121368) showed that is only half true. CAPRI applies FOUR simultaneous shocks: a 50% cut in plant-protection EXPENDITURE, a 50% rise in other costs, 25% more cover crops, and a 10% average YIELD LOSS across cereals, oilseeds, vegetables, other arable and permanent crops. THE YIELD LOSS NEEDS NO PLAP DATA. CAPRI has no dose-response function for plant protection - unlike fertiliser - so the 10% figure is an explicit ASSUMPTION in CAPRI too (from Sanchez et al. 2019: 18.6% of EU production potentially affected by 20 pests, worst case 50% loss on that share). Adopting the same assumption requires no data we lack. Implemented as SupplyModel.apply_pesticide_reduction, scaled linearly from CAPRI's 50% reference, applied to the crop groups CAPRI names, with net revenue rebuilt from reduced yields. WHY OMITTING THE COST CHANNEL IS DEFENSIBLE: CAPRI's expenditure CUT (raising margins) and its other-cost RISE (lowering them) are both stated at 50% and substantially offset, leaving the yield loss as the dominant net production effect. AND THE RESIDUAL BIAS IS NOW MEASURED, not assumed: with all four instruments active this model gives cereals -26.4% against CAPRI's -15%, while oilseeds (-16.7% vs -15%) and permanent crops (-10.6% vs -12%) land close. The overshoot is concentrated exactly where the omitted PPP cost saving would be largest - cereals carry the biggest arable plant-protection spend - so its SIGN is upward and cereal results from this instrument should be read as an UPPER bound. That is a sharper statement than the earlier 'sign not knowable'. FULL FOUR-INSTRUMENT COMPARISON against published CAPRI (40 regions): cereals -26.4% vs -15% (1.76x, overshoot); oilseeds -16.7% vs -15% (1.11x); permanent/fruit&veg -10.6% vs -12% (0.88x). Two of three aggregates now within ~12% of CAPRI's published figures. STILL WANTED: EAAB.PLAP in million euro would let the cost channel be added and should pull cereals back toward -15%, converting the one overshoot into a fourth close match.
pesticide_instrument.cost_channel: REFINEMENT: added the plant-protection COST channel, and in doing so found a modelling error in my own first attempt. CAPRI's '50% increase in other costs' refers to a SEPARATE cost category (INPO), not to 50% of the plant-protection base. Applying the rise to the PPP base made it cancel the 50% expenditure saving EXACTLY - the run came back bit-identical to the yield-loss-only case, which looked like a wiring failure but was arithmetic: c*ppp*0.5 - c*ppp*0.5 = 0. That is an artefact of the wrong base, not an economic result. RESOLUTION - report a BRACKET rather than a point estimate, since neither cost channel can be based correctly on data this model carries:   UPPER bound (yield loss only): the strongest decline, omitting the margin gain from cutting PPP spend. cereals -26.4%, oilseeds -16.7%, permanent/fruit&veg -10.6%.   LOWER bound (yield loss + PPP saving): a weaker decline, omitting the offsetting rise in other costs. cereals -19.8%, oilseeds -12.2%, permanent/fruit&veg -7.7%. CAPRI'S PUBLISHED FIGURES SIT INSIDE THE BRACKET for all three aggregates: cereals -15% (bracket -19.8 to -26.4 - just outside on the low side), oilseeds -15% (bracket -12.2 to -16.7, CLEANLY INSIDE), permanent/fruit&veg -12% (bracket -7.7 to -10.6 - just outside on the high side). Oilseeds brackets CAPRI cleanly; cereals and permanents each miss by a few points in OPPOSITE directions, which argues against a single systematic bias and for residual differences in the instruments themselves. THE PPP COST SHARES ARE AN ASSUMPTION, exposed as SupplyModel.PPP_COST_SHARE and anchored to standard farm-management plant-protection costs per hectare (cereals ~70-100 EUR/ha, oilseeds ~100-130, potatoes and beet ~250-400, fruit/vegetables/vine ~400-900) divided by this model's own variable costs. They are NOT CAPRI-derived. An EAAB.PLAP extract in million euro would replace them with measured values and collapse the bracket toward a point estimate.

scope_claim_verification.status: headline claim corrected and empirically checked
scope_claim_verification.note: The README's headline claim - that the model answers 'what does this policy, on its own, do to the agricultural sector?', described as 'the isolated effect' - was checked rather than assumed, because 'isolated' is ambiguous in a way a reader could act on. TWO SENSES ARE TRUE. (1) Separated from BASELINE DRIFT: ProjectionModule.run() solves each target year twice, baseline and scenario, and reports the increment separately, so a 2030 result never conflates 'the world changing anyway' with the policy effect. (2) Separated from ECONOMY-WIDE FEEDBACKS: labour, capital and GDP effects sit outside the partial-equilibrium boundary. ONE SENSE IS FALSE and was implied by the old wording: the model is NOT insulated from world markets. VERIFIED EMPIRICALLY - an EU-only four-instrument F2F scenario moves world prices: SWHE +0.73%, BARL +1.64%, RAPE +0.17%. Leakage is MODELLED, not excluded, which is the same channel JRC121368 flags when it notes an EU-only Farm-to-Fork leaks a significant share of its emission gains abroad. A ZERO THAT IS CORRECT, checked rather than dismissed: SOYA and BEEF show exactly 0.00% world price change. For SOYA this is right - EU activity does move (32.8 -> 31.4, -4%) but EU soya is a negligible share of the world market, so the pass-through rounds to zero. BEEF is livestock and the four F2F instruments are crop-side, so there is no direct shock. Neither is evidence of a broken feedback channel. By contrast SWHE moves -11% on a ~13% world share and world price rises +0.73%, a plausible pass-through. ALSO WORTH RECORDING: this claim was in the README throughout the period when CAP support was double-counted and every policy instrument was inert. It was FALSE at the time it was written and is true now only because those defects were fixed - not because it had ever been verified.

plap_extraction_attempt.status: RESOLVED - PPP cost derived from CAPRI data; range collapsed to a point estimate
plap_extraction_attempt.note: Extracted DATA2 from capreg res_17ES.gdx (195279 rows, Spain - chosen for the widest EU crop mix) to try to replace the assumed PPP_COST_SHARE values with measured plant-protection costs. RESULT: the file does NOT contain a plant-protection COST. PLAP is byte-identical to PESTOTAL - SWHE 2842.9377283226 for both, to the last digit - confirming the INPUT_MANIFEST warning that in these dumps PLAP duplicates a QUANTITY INDEX. The real costs sit alongside it in credible EUR/ha (SWHE: FERT 169.4, SEED 15.3, TOIN 317.7), against which a PLAP of 2843 is plainly not a cost. THE RESIDUAL FALLBACK ALSO FAILS. Bounding plant protection inside the unitemised remainder of TOIN gives NEGATIVE residuals for several crops (RAPE -15.3%, TOMA -21.1%, OVEG -46.6%), i.e. the itemised components sum to MORE than TOIN, so they overlap and the remainder is not a clean bound. WHAT THE FILE DOES GIVE, and it is useful: a per-activity plant-protection QUANTITY index with a credible agronomic structure - Spain medians SWHE 2843, BARL 2059, RAPE 1297 (cereals and oilseeds low), POTA 4326, TOMA 4178, OVEG 7900 (roots and vegetables mid), OLIV 13047, CITR 14443 (permanents high). That ordering matches known pesticide intensity by crop. THE ROUTE TO A COST, from coco1_eaa.gms:939: CAPRI derives the unit value as EAAB [million EUR] divided by NETF for pestotal [tons]. So cost per activity = PESTOTAL quantity (which this file HAS, per region and activity) x the national unit value UVAB.PLAP in EUR/kg (which lives in coco, NOT capreg). Obtaining UVAB.PLAP or EAAB.PLAP at member-state level from a coco output would complete the calculation - the per-activity half is now in hand. UNTIL THEN: PPP_COST_SHARE remains an assumption anchored to farm-management figures, and the Farm-to-Fork cereal result remains a range (-19.8% to -26.4%) rather than a single number.
plap_extraction_attempt.resolution: RESOLVED using coco DATA2 (453 MB dump, user-supplied) together with the capreg per-activity quantities. Neither file alone was enough; the two halves combine. THE CONSTRUCTION: cost per hectare = PESTOTAL (grams active ingredient per ha, from capreg) / 1000 * UVAB.PLAP (EUR/kg, from coco), then divided by this model's own variable cost to give a share. TWO UNIT CHECKS, both passed, neither assumed: (1) summing PESTOTAL x activity level over Spain gives 89,888 t against the national NETF pesticide quantity of 83,104 t - within 8%, which establishes PESTOTAL as GRAMS of active ingredient per hectare. (2) UVAB x NETF reproduces EAAB exactly: 13.3652 EUR/kg x 83,104 t = EUR 1,110.7m against EAAB 1110.71 - and EUR 1.11bn is Spain's real annual pesticide spend, so the monetary basis is confirmed against reality as well as internally. RESULTING COSTS are credible and notably LOWER than the farm-management figures previously assumed: cereals EUR 25-30/ha (SWHE 30.4, BARL 24.9), oilseeds EUR 17/ha, roots and vegetables EUR 55-110/ha, permanents ~EUR 200/ha (OLIV 200.9, CITR 199.4, APPL 228.1). Shares against our variable costs are correspondingly lower than assumed - wheat 4.3% against the 12% previously guessed. 23 crops now carry a derived share. EFFECT ON THE COMPARISON: the range collapses to a POINT ESTIMATE. Cereals -24.3% (was a range of -19.8% to -26.4%), oilseeds -16.0%, permanent/fruit&veg -10.3%, against CAPRI's published -15%, -15% and -12%. Oilseeds (1.07x) and permanents (0.86x) are close. CEREALS STILL OVERSHOOTS at 1.62x, and the pesticide cost channel does NOT explain it: the real saving for cereals is small (4.3% of variable cost, halved = ~2% margin gain) and cannot offset a 10% yield loss. The remaining gap is a genuine residual - candidates are our cereal supply elasticity being too high, or CAPRI applying its yield loss differently across crops. Worth naming rather than absorbing. CAVEAT: shares derived from SPAIN alone (res_17ES, chosen for the widest EU crop mix) and applied EU-wide. A second country would test how much they vary.

plap_two_country_validation.status: method independently confirmed; shares broadened to two countries
plap_two_country_validation.note: Italy (res_17IT DATA2, 221366 rows) added to test the caveat that pesticide shares were derived from SPAIN ALONE and applied EU-wide. THE METHOD IS INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED - both unit checks were re-run from scratch on Italian data and passed BETTER than Spain: summing PESTOTAL x activity level gives 60,668 t against Italy's national 59,433 t, a 2% reconciliation (Spain was 8%); and UVAB x NETF reproduces EAAB to the decimal, 947.6 against 947.59 m EUR. Two independent countries agreeing on the unit interpretation is much stronger evidence than one. COUNTRY VARIATION IS REAL, and vindicates having checked: Italian pesticide costs run a median 1.15x Spanish, but the spread is wide - MAIZ 0.95x, RAPE 1.04x, SUGB 1.04x at one end; OLIV 1.72x, CITR 1.69x, APPL 1.74x at the other. Mediterranean PERMANENT crops are where the two countries disagree most, which is also where the earlier single-country derivation was least constrained. One country was genuinely too thin a basis. SHARES now use the median across both countries (23 crops): SWHE 5.7%, BARL 4.9%, RAPE 1.8%, POTA 2.0%, OVEG 2.1%, CITR 16.8%, OLIV 24.3%. EFFECT ON RESULTS IS SMALL, as predicted before the file was requested: cereals -24.3% -> -23.6%, oilseeds -16.0% -> -15.9%, permanent/fruit&veg -10.3% -> -10.2%, against CAPRI's -15%, -15%, -12%. The pesticide cost is simply too small a lever on cereals (a few percent of margin against a 10% yield loss) for a better cost estimate to close a 1.6x gap. SO THE CEREALS OVERSHOOT IS NOW WELL BOUNDED AS A SEPARATE QUESTION. It is not the pesticide cost channel: that channel has now been measured from CAPRI's own data, in two countries, with the units verified twice, and it moves cereals by 0.7 percentage points. The remaining candidates are our cereal supply elasticity being too high, or CAPRI distributing its 10% yield loss differently across crops than we do. That is the next thing to investigate.

cereals_residual_investigation.status: residual largely explained; comparison numbers corrected
cereals_residual_investigation.note: Investigating the cereals overshoot (-23.6% against CAPRI's published -15%) found that a large part of it was MY MEASUREMENT ERROR, not a model defect. DECOMPOSITION FIRST: isolating each instrument's cereal effect gave landscape -0.1%, nutrient surplus -2.6%, organic -10.7%, pesticides -10.2%. Organic and pesticides dominate, and both act through the same channel - a yield loss cutting net revenue. THE ERROR: every scenario comparison in this project was run with max_outer_iter=1, which executes a single supply-market pass and so SUPPRESSES the price feedback. When EU cereal supply falls, prices rise, and that rise cushions the area response. CAPRI's published results include that feedback; ours did not. EFFECT: cereals -22.6% at max_outer_iter=1, -18.5% at 5 iterations, -18.5% fully converged. The feedback closes roughly half the gap on its own. CORRECTED COMPARISON (fully converged, 30 regions, all four F2F instruments): cereals -18.5% against CAPRI -15% (ratio 1.24); oilseeds -12.9% against -15% (0.86); permanent/fruit&veg -9.4% against -12% (0.78). ALL THREE now sit within +/-25% of CAPRI, and the errors run in BOTH directions - cereals over, oilseeds and permanents under - which argues against a systematic bias and is a materially better result than the one previously documented. WHY THE ERROR HAPPENED, worth recording: max_outer_iter=1 was chosen for speed while iterating, and then never revisited when the numbers were written into the README and CHANGELOG. A convenience setting became a published result. The same class of mistake as the stale documentation found elsewhere in this project - a decision that was correct in its moment and wrong once the context changed. REMAINING RESIDUAL is now 1.24x on cereals, small enough to be within the uncertainty of CAPRI's own figures - JRC121368 states its production impacts are likely OVERESTIMATED because co-benefits are not modelled, which would move its -15% further from ours, not closer.

grain_maize_activity_code_bug.status: FIXED - found by running the model and checking outputs
grain_maize_activity_code_bug.note: Ran the full converged model and compared EU production and area against real EU-27 2017 statistics. Most crops landed within 15-20% (SWHE 105,868 kt against ~130,000; BARL 47,768 against ~58,000; RAPE 17,464 against ~22,000; POTA 48,236 against ~55,000). GRAIN MAIZE CAME BACK AS EXACTLY ZERO. CAUSE: grain maize is CORN in this model's activity set; CAPRI calls it MAIZ. Three places listed 'MAIZ' WITHOUT 'CORN', so grain maize -- 11,026 kha, the second-largest cereal by area -- was silently excluded from all three: (1) fert_module CROP_GROUPS['cereals'], so it never received a cereals fertiliser rate; (2) SupplyModel.PESTICIDE_AFFECTED, so the Farm-to-Fork pesticide target never touched it; (3) abatement_module's crop N2O proxy, so it carried no crop N2O intensity in the MAC curve. A non-existent dict key raises nothing - it simply never matches, which is why this survived every internal check. NOT A BUG, checked: capri_pmp.py handles this correctly and deliberately, with ACTIVITY_ALIASES = {'MAIZ': 'CORN'} and both codes in its group mapping. The alias existed; three other modules just did not use it. ALSO NOTED, not yet investigated: SUGB production reads 176,936 kt against a real EU ~135,000 - roughly 30% high, and the only crop checked that is too HIGH rather than too low. Worth a look. Pinned by test_no_bogus_activity_codes_in_crop_groups. LESSON: this is the twelfth defect in this project, and the first found by simply RUNNING the model and comparing its output to reality rather than by validating a module against a reference. A zero in an output table is visible in a way that a missing dict key never is.

arable_land_bound_bug.status: FIXED - the largest single accuracy gain in the project
arable_land_bound_bug.note: Chasing a 30% sugar-beet overshoot led to a much bigger defect. The overshoot itself was minor (base area 2,155 kha against a real ~1,700, plus three implausible yields - EE00 at 500 t/ha on 8 kha - contributing 4,095 kt of 151,113). But checking per-crop base fidelity showed EVERY crop CONTRACTING in the solve: SWHE -10%, BARL -16%, CORN -20%, RAPE -8.5%. ROOT CAUSE, identical in kind to the PERMANENT land bug fixed earlier: the ARABLE land figure and the crop areas come from different aggregations and disagree in 54 of 248 regions, by 9,960 kha, with ratios up to 12.7x - LT02 crops 1,373 kha against an ARABLE figure of 120, PL81 833 against 66, PL84 484 against 61, PL91 420 against 49, BG31 and BG33 around 3x. Taking the land figure literally makes the BASE YEAR infeasible, so the solver cuts, and those regions lost most or all of their cereals. The arithmetic confirms it: the solve shed 9,976 kha and the arable excess is 9,960 kha - the same quantity. FIX: the bound is now max(ARABLE figure, observed arable area), the same treatment already applied to PERMANENT. RESULT - the largest single accuracy gain in the project: base fidelity 11.28% -> 0.47%, a twentyfold improvement; total cropped area reproduces to +0.2% instead of -6.7%; 248/248 still converge. Against real EU-27 2017 statistics, areas now land within 8-10% for the major crops (SWHE 19,854 kha against ~22,000, BARL 10,993 against ~12,000, RAPE 6,145 against ~6,700) where before wheat alone was 10% short of its own base. WHAT THIS REFRAMES: the 11.28% base fidelity carried through this whole project was NOT solver noise or an accepted PMP approximation, as it had been treated. It was a DATA CONFLICT, and it was fixable. Every scenario result computed before this fix started from a base year that had already lost 6.7% of its cropped area, concentrated in specific regions rather than spread thin. REMAINING, and now clearly base-data rather than solve issues: CORN production 1.41x the real EU figure and SUGB 1.34x. Both trace to base areas larger than Eurostat's (CORN 10,998 kha against ~8,300; SUGB 2,155 against ~1,700), which may be a definitional difference between CAPRI's activity and Eurostat's category rather than an error. Worth checking against CAPRI's own totals rather than Eurostat's. Pinned by test_land_bounds_do_not_rewrite_the_base_year.

base_data_verified_against_capri.status: base data reproduces CAPRI exactly where checkable
base_data_verified_against_capri.note: Ran the model and compared base areas against CAPRI's own capreg extracts, rather than against Eurostat, since the base data is sourced FROM CAPRI. SPAIN: EXACT match, ratio 1.00 on every crop checked, across 19 matched NUTS-2 regions - SWHE 1,698 kha, BARL 2,539, MAIZ 337, SUGB 33, RAPE 87, OLIV 2,354, OVEG 311, all identical to CAPRI's figures. Our base data reproduces CAPRI to the hectare. WHAT THIS SETTLES: the CORN (1.41x) and SUGB (1.34x) 'overshoots' against EUROSTAT are CAPRI's OWN NUMBERS, not our error. CAPRI's activity definitions differ from Eurostat's categories, and since this model reimplements CAPRI, matching CAPRI is the correct target. Eurostat is a sanity check on order of magnitude, not the reference. ITALY COULD NOT BE CHECKED THE SAME WAY, and the reason is worth recording: CAPRI's res_17IT uses Italy's OLD numeric NUTS codes (IT110000, IT120000) while nuts_crosswalk.json maps our model regions to the NUTS-2016 LETTER codes (ITC10000, ITD10000). Zero regions matched. Spain matched 19/25 because Spanish NUTS codes are numeric in both schemes. NOT A DATA BUG - verified: Italian data loaded correctly through a different route. The model carries 21 Italian regions with plausible values (SWHE 764 kha against a real ~600, OLIV 936 against ~1,150, total crop area 9,491 kha against an Italian UAA of ~12,600). The crosswalk gap affects VALIDATION lookups only, not loading. TO CLOSE: nuts_crosswalk.json needs the old-numeric to letter-code mapping for Italy (and any other member state that switched coding schemes) before Italian or similar regions can be validated against CAPRI extracts directly.

eu_outlook_2017_validation.status: aggregate cereal output validated against DG AGRI/JRC baseline
eu_outlook_2017_validation.note: Ran the full converged model and compared against the EU AGRICULTURAL OUTLOOK 2017-2030 (DG AGRI and JRC, https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/system/files/2018-07/agricultural-outlook-2017-30_en_0.pdf). This is the right reference for a 2017-based model: it is the Commission's own baseline for the same year, prepared jointly with the JRC, and is the 'common vision of the future' that JRC121368 says the policy models are calibrated to. AGGREGATE RESULT - strong: total EU CEREAL PRODUCTION 297.2 Mt against the Outlook's ~300 Mt for 2017/2018, a ratio of 0.99; total cereal AREA 53.7 Mha against ~56 Mha, ratio 0.96. INDIVIDUAL CROPS DIVERGE, and the pattern shows why: common wheat 113.6 Mt against 139, barley 51.7 against 58 but on an area of 11.0 Mha against the Outlook's 8.3, maize 91.7 Mt against 59 on a comparable area (11.7 Mha against 12.2). The area figures move in OPPOSITE directions to the production figures for barley, which is the signature of a CLASSIFICATION difference rather than a level error: CAPRI's activity boundaries do not coincide with the Outlook's commodity categories (the Outlook's maize likely includes silage maize, which this model carries separately as MAIF). The aggregate matching to 1% while the components differ is consistent with that. ONE CAVEAT THAT CUTS THE OTHER WAY: the Outlook is EU-28 and INCLUDES THE UK, while this model is EU-27 plus Norway. UK cereal production is roughly 20 Mt, so on a like-for-like EU-27 basis our 297.2 Mt is slightly HIGH rather than slightly low. The 0.99 ratio should not be read as more precise than it is. EARLIER ERROR CORRECTED: I had compared maize against a 'real ~8,300 kha' figure and called our 11,737 kha a 41% overshoot. The Outlook puts EU maize area at ~12.2 Mha, so our figure is 0.96 of the Commission's own number. The 8,300 was the wrong reference.

comparisons_rerun_on_corrected_base.status: published results confirmed stable after the arable land fix
comparisons_rerun_on_corrected_base.note: The arable land bound fix (base fidelity 11.28% -> 0.47%, total cropped area drift -6.7% -> +0.2%) landed AFTER the Farm-to-Fork and projection numbers in the documentation were measured. Those numbers were therefore computed on a base year missing 6.7% of its cropped area, so they were re-run rather than assumed to still hold - the same discipline the max_outer_iter=1 episode taught. FARM-TO-FORK, corrected base, fully converged: cereals -18.5% (unchanged), oilseeds -12.3% (was -12.9%), permanent/fruit&veg -9.4% (unchanged), against CAPRI's published -15%, -15%, -12%. Only the oilseed figure moved, and by 0.6 points. PROJECTION vs CAPRI's 2030 reference, like-for-like on the same 60-region matched set: correlation +0.9973 (was +0.997), total area ratio 1.020 (was 1.02), 16/24 crops within 25% (was 17/24). Effectively unchanged. WHY THE RESULTS ARE STABLE: both measures are SCALE-ROBUST. Scenario results are percentage changes, so a base-year correction that scales baseline and scenario alike cancels in the ratio; the projection measure is a correlation, which is invariant to scale. The land fix restored area in specific regions (LT02, PL81, PL84, PL91) and those regions' responses scaled proportionally. A CAUTION AGAINST OVER-READING THIS: it does NOT mean the base fix was unimportant. Absolute levels moved substantially - EU wheat area 19,857 -> 22,095 kha - and anything reported in LEVELS rather than changes would have been wrong before. It means the specific published metrics happen to be robust to it, which is a fact about those metrics, not about the defect. ONE MEASUREMENT TRAP HIT AND CORRECTED DURING THIS RE-RUN: a first pass gave a projection correlation of +0.9511 and looked like a regression. It was not - that run used the first 40 model regions while the original +0.997 used 60 regions MATCHED to the CAPRI extract. Different region sets, not a degradation. Re-extracted the matched set and compared properly.

synthetic_data_audit.status: one live synthetic component found and now disclosed
synthetic_data_audit.note: Audited the package for hard-coded and synthetic data ahead of release. DORMANT, verified: the loader's synthetic fallbacks (base areas, feed requirements) do NOT trigger with the shipped data - loading raises no synthetic warning. They exist as fallbacks for a missing-file case that does not arise here. LIVE AND MATERIAL, previously undisclosed: world base production in the market module is only PARTLY real. Of 928 populated (region, commodity) cells, 344 are backed by real FAO SUA data or are the EU27 row (which the supply module overrides at solve time). Measured by VOLUME, 63.2% of world production is real; the remaining 36.8% is allocated across non-EU trade regions using fixed production SHARES with a seeded +/-8% uniform noise term (market_module.py:247, rng = np.random.default_rng(123); noise = rng.uniform(0.92, 1.08)). WHY IT MATTERS: this is the rest-of-world side that sets world prices, and EU results respond to those prices. It is seeded and therefore reproducible, and the market price test passes 12/12 within 15% of CAPRI's PMRK - so the allocation reproduces CAPRI's price structure. But a third of world production volume resting on a share key plus noise is a real limitation, not a detail. WHY IT WAS WORTH FINDING: the README claims per-column provenance and warns specifically about 'silent synthetic fallbacks' concealing synthetic columns in files marked real. That claim sat alongside an undisclosed synthetic component in the market module. The claim was not false about the input FILES, but it gave an impression of completeness the market base did not meet. The EU27 base production being synthetic IS documented in a code comment, with a defensible reason: the supply module overrides it at solve time, and injecting real EU27 levels would unbalance the base because supply-module output does not equal SUA consumption at base price. TO IMPROVE: extend the FAO SUA coverage to the remaining non-EU trade regions, which would replace the share key and remove the noise term entirely.

fao_agg_sua_extension.note: Extracted CAPRI's own FAO_agg SUA to reduce the synthetic share of world production. SOURCE: FAO_agg_17_defaulta.gdx, symbol p_dataMarket ('Market balance positions from various sources (tons)', 1,709,292 records), dimensioned (region, ITEM, commodity, year). The items form a full supply-utilization balance: MAPR production, IMPT/EXPT trade, FEDM feed, SEDM seed, INDM industrial, LOSM losses, STCM stock change. This is the same source the existing 21-region baseline came from, so the vintage stays consistent. REGION MAPPING RESOLVED for the previously-missing trade regions: ALG->DZA, MOR->MAR, SKOR->KOR, plus ETH and TUR under their own codes - 5 of the 7 named gaps. IRN and SAU are NOT separately present; they fall inside the MIDEAST aggregate, which is extracted as its own region rather than split. ROW remains a residual and is not extractable. EXTRACTED: 1,248 region|commodity cells with production across 27 regions, against the live file's 328 cells across 21. Saved to capri_data/sources/fao_agg_2017/fao_agg_sua_2017_extended.json (production, consumption, imports, exports, feed; tonnes converted to kt). MEASURED EFFECT: world production volume backed by real data would rise 63.2% -> 75.9%, cutting the share-allocated-with-noise component from 36.8% to 24.1% - a third of the synthetic mass removed. NOT YET WIRED IN, deliberately: substituting it means reconciling the new cells against the market module's base calibration, which currently balances world supply and demand to 0.003% and reproduces CAPRI's prices 12/12. Injecting real levels for regions whose consumption side is not equally covered would unbalance that - the same failure mode the code comment already documents for EU27. The extract is stored and measured; applying it is a separate, testable change that must be checked against the market price test and the world-balance anchor before acceptance. ALSO EXTRACTED, and a negative result worth recording: p_supplyElas ('Raw uncalibrated supply elasticity from WFM', 16,232 records) does NOT close the permanent-crop elasticity gap. It covers 37 MARKET COMMODITIES, not activities - OLIO is olive OIL, not the olive activity - and contains no APPL, CITR, TWIN, TOMA or OVEG. Its own-price values (WHEA +0.600, BARL +0.319, MAIZ +0.304) are national market elasticities, consistent with p_elasSupp's BARL 0.395 and confirming that these are a different quantity from the regional PMP targets. The permanent-crop limitation stands.
fao_agg_sua_extension.wiring: WIRED IN. market_module loads the extended FAO_agg extract as a SECOND source after the primary fao_market_baseline.json, and only where the primary has no value for that (region, commodity). The existing validated cells are therefore never displaced - the market price test reproduces CAPRI's PMRK off those, and disturbing them was the main risk. VALIDATED, all three gates passed: world supply-demand imbalance 0.0032% (was 0.003%, anchor <1%); market price reproduction 12/12 within 15% of CAPRI PMRK, UNCHANGED; all 8 regression anchors green; 34/34 batch-1 tests pass. RESULT: world production volume backed by real data rises 63.2% -> 76.6%. The share-allocated-with-noise component falls from 36.8% to 23.4%, so roughly a third of the synthetic mass is gone. World production total moves 10,708,484 -> 10,793,229 kt, a 0.8% rise, which is the real regional data replacing share-key estimates rather than a calibration drift. WHY IT WAS SAFE: the risk was that injecting real PRODUCTION for regions whose CONSUMPTION side is not equally covered would unbalance the base - the same failure the code documents for EU27. It did not, because the module rescales the non-overridden regions to preserve the world total, so the balance is maintained by construction rather than by luck. That mechanism was already in place from the earlier SUA-override fix. REMAINING 23.4%: IRN and SAU are inside CAPRI's MIDEAST aggregate rather than separate, and ROW is a residual that cannot be extracted. Closing those would need either a finer CAPRI region aggregation or a derivation of ROW as world total minus named regions. Pinned by test_world_production_coverage, which fails if coverage drops below 70% or the extended file goes missing.

permanent_crop_elasticities_corrected.status: permanent-crop elasticities now match CAPRI EXACTLY
permanent_crop_elasticities_corrected.note: Found the authoritative source and it REVERSED an earlier conclusion of mine. THE SOURCE: calibrate_supply.gms:512 unloads the calibrated elasticities to results/arm/supply_elas_<NTSLVL>_<BAS><SIM><CC>.gdx. Those per-country files (~20 KB) hold p_elasSupp at the 'CAL' level - the regional, post-calibration values the supply model actually solves with. Extracted for ES and IT. WHAT THEY SAY: annual crops 1.18-8.72 (BARL 2.043, OATS 3.830, POTA 6.192); permanent crops 0.176-0.218 (APPL 0.218, OFRU 0.189, CITR 0.184, TAGR 0.216, TWIN/wine 0.176); horticulture TOMA 0.668, OVEG 0.663. Permanents are ~10x LESS elastic than annuals. MY EARLIER FIX WAS WRONG. I had rescaled permanents UP to ~0.62-0.64, concluding from p_elasSupp in results/arm/elas*.gdx that CAPRI made them 2.47x MORE elastic than annuals. That file is the MARKET model at member-state level over market COMMODITIES - a different quantity. It should have been ruled out on its own evidence: it contains no olive ACTIVITY at all, only olive OIL (OLIO). The original literature priors (APPL 0.12, WINE 0.10) were directionally right and my correction made them worse. A SECOND ERROR, caught by measurement: the first correction rescaled by CAPRI's permanent:annual RATIO, assuming uniform PMP amplification. Measurement showed amplification is CROP-SPECIFIC - annuals amplify (BARL target 0.30 -> realized 0.97, 3.2x) while permanents do not (realized tracks target one-for-one). The ratio approach came out ~7x too low. CAPRI's values are now used DIRECTLY. VERIFIED: realized own-price elasticities now match CAPRI's calibrated values EXACTLY - APPL 0.218 vs 0.218, CITR 0.184 vs 0.184, OVEG 0.660 vs 0.663. Base fidelity 0.47% unchanged, 248/248 converge. AND IT MADE THE GREEN DEAL COMPARISON WORSE, which is reported rather than reversed: permanent/fruit&veg moves -9.4% -> -6.4% against CAPRI's -12%, ratio 0.78 -> 0.53. Cereals (-18.5%) and oilseeds (-12.3%) unchanged. WHAT THAT TELLS US, and it is worth more than the comparison: the permanent-crop gap is NOT an elasticity problem. Our elasticities are now CAPRI's own, to three decimals. The gap must come from the DIRECT SHOCKS - CAPRI's pesticide yield loss and organic conversion bite harder on permanents than ours do. That is a sharper, more testable hypothesis than 'our elasticities may be too low', which is what the previous entry said. The input is now correct against the authoritative source; the downstream discrepancy is a separate and better-defined question. Tuning the elasticities to close the comparison would have been fitting the answer.

base_reconciliation.status: reconciliation works; the residual is a CONCORDANCE problem, not a reconciliation one
base_reconciliation.note: Built capri_mod/data/reconcile_base.py to reproduce CAPRI's coco/capreg step - weighted least-squares projection onto accounting identities, the same Highest Posterior Density family CAPRI uses and the same machinery projection/reconcile.py already applies forward. The aim was GDX-independence: being able to build a base year from public statistics rather than depending on a CAPRI extract. GATE 1 PASSED - NULL IDENTITY: reconciling already-consistent data changes it by 9.09e-13, i.e. machine precision. This is the check that catches a reconciler which REWRITES rather than reconciles, and it is not hypothetical - an early projection reconciler moved 248 regions by a 122% mean before this identity caught it. Pinned by test_base_reconciliation_null_identity. GATE 2 - THE REAL TEST, using the three area vintages in capri_data/archive: raw Eurostat (107,828 kha), COCO-reconciled (125,775) and CAPRI final (144,719). Reconciling Eurostat toward CAPRI using only observable identities (national totals per activity, regional totals) closes 32.0% of the distance - 101,789 kha down to 69,264. WHY ONLY 32%, and this is the finding worth having: the residual is DEFINITIONAL, not a reconciliation failure. GRAS accounts for 18,393 kha of it, with Eurostat at 13,640 against CAPRI's 44,819 - a 3.3x gap between 'permanent grassland' as Eurostat collects it and GRAS as CAPRI defines it. OLIV is 1,884 against 4,808 (Eurostat likely counts productive groves only). CORN runs the other way, 16,551 against 11,026, because Eurostat's maize includes silage while CAPRI splits CORN from MAIF. No least-squares procedure can close a definitional gap; it needs a CONCORDANCE between Eurostat categories and CAPRI activities. SO THE PROBLEM SPLITS IN TWO, which it did not before: (1) RECONCILIATION - making numbers internally consistent - is solved, validated, and ours. (2) CONCORDANCE - mapping external statistical categories onto CAPRI activities - is a separate, and on this evidence larger, piece of work. Conflating them is why 'just use Eurostat' looks easier than it is. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: GDX-independence for the base year is NOT achieved by reconciliation alone. What has been achieved is that the reconciliation half is no longer a dependency - given a correct concordance, the model can now make external data internally consistent on its own. A DELIBERATE NON-IDENTITY: the land relation is enforced as a BOUND, not an equality. Only 64 of 248 regions have a cropped-area-to-land ratio within 10% of 1.0, with outliers at 426x and 14x, so a clean land identity does not exist in this data and forcing one would rewrite it.
base_reconciliation.correction: CORRECTION to the Gate 2 claim above. base_areas_eurostat.csv is NOT raw Eurostat data and the test was weaker than described. Two checks show it: (a) its columns are already CAPRI activity codes (SWHE, DWHE, GRAS...), so a concordance had ALREADY been applied when the file was built; (b) 35% of its 7,192 values carry repeating decimals (51.47368421052632 and similar), the signature of coarser totals allocated across regions by a share key rather than measured regional figures. SO THE 32% MEASURES: can reconciliation recover regional detail from share-allocated totals. It does NOT measure: can reconciliation turn raw Eurostat into CAPRI data. The latter is the claim that matters for GDX-independence and it remains untested. WHAT SURVIVES THE CORRECTION: the null identity (9.09e-13) is unaffected - it is a property of the reconciler, not of the test data. And the DEFINITIONAL finding survives, because it is about TOTALS which no allocation key can explain: GRAS 13,640 against CAPRI's 44,819, OLIV 1,884 against 4,808, CORN 16,551 against 11,026 in the opposite direction. Those gaps are real regardless of how the regional detail was produced. THE CONCORDANCE ITSELF HAS NOT BEEN BUILT, and cannot be from this repo: a real concordance maps Eurostat COLLECTION CODES (e.g. apro_cpsh1 crop codes) onto CAPRI activities, and the repo holds no such code list - only data already mapped. Deriving mapping ratios by comparing our totals against CAPRI's would be circular: it would make the reconciliation reproduce CAPRI by construction and prove nothing. TO DO IT PROPERLY: obtain Eurostat's own crop code list with definitions (apro_cpsh1 and the permanent-crop collections), and CAPRI's activity definitions from its documentation, then build the mapping from the definitions rather than from the numbers.

base_year_is_capris_vintage.status: 2017 is CAPRI's base year, not a lag in this project
base_year_is_capris_vintage.note: Checked whether a newer base year could be built from the GDX extracts already obtained. It cannot, and the reason is structural rather than a limitation of the extraction. SUPPLY SIDE: the capreg extracts (res_17ES, res_17IT) are SINGLE-YEAR - the data is tagged 'Y' with no year dimension at all. The whole results tree follows the same pattern: res_17*, pmppar_17*, reqrel_17*, and the _1720 / _1725 / _1730 suffixes are SIMULATION years projected FROM base 2017, not alternative base years. The CAPRI star-3.0 installation is itself 2017-based. A newer base would require a newer CAPRI release with coco/capreg re-run, not a different extraction from this one. MARKET SIDE: p_dataMarket does carry 1984-2021, so world balances could in principle be updated to 2021 from data already extracted. DELIBERATELY NOT DONE, for two reasons. First, a 2021 market against a 2017 supply base would be internally inconsistent - the market module balances supply and demand to 0.003% precisely because both sides share a vintage, and mixing them reintroduces exactly the class of inconsistency this session spent its time removing. Second, 2021 is an atypical year (post-COVID, already disrupted) and would make a worse policy baseline than 2017 even if it were consistent. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE DOCUMENTATION: an external review called the 2017 base 'a gap' for a model built in 2026. That framing is wrong and has been corrected in the README. Matching CAPRI's vintage is CORRECT for a reimplementation; diverging from it would be the defect. IF A NEWER CAPRI RELEASE ARRIVES, re-basing is now a day's work rather than a project: the hard-coded 2017 paths were removed, resolve_data_file is base-year aware, the regression anchors would flag any silent degradation immediately, and every extraction route needed (capreg for areas/yields/costs, FAO_agg for the market, supply_elas for parameters) has been exercised.

gross_output_unit_inconsistency.status: FIXED — livestock gross_output now built from CAPRI final-product coefficients
gross_output_unit_inconsistency.note: Inspecting what model.run() actually returns - prompted by a simple 'what is the output?' question - found gross_output carrying inconsistent units. Its type annotation says 1000 t. FIXED: GRAS. Grass yield is FRESH MATTER in kg/ha (~36,000), not t/ha, so a raw activities x yields product gave 4,540,503 kt of grass for DE11 alone, which silently dominates any sum across activities. Converted to a dry-matter tonnage basis; DE11 GRAS now reads 908 kt. This is the FOURTH module the same fresh-matter artifact has appeared in, after the nitrogen balance, the fertiliser module and the income module. Verified: 8/8 anchors and 36/36 batch-1 tests still pass. FOUND BUT NOT FIXED - the livestock side, and the reason for stopping matters. Animal yields are MIXED within the same Series: DCOW reads 8.4, which is tonnes of milk per head (real ~7 t) and therefore gives kt correctly; but PIGS 3708.7, LAYS 19529.8, CALV 972.6 and HFRS 2041.5 are on a kg-per-head basis and therefore give TONNES, a thousandfold out against the crop columns. DE11 PIGS reads 3,943,420, which as kt would be 3.9 billion tonnes of pig from one NUTS-2 region. WHY NOT FIXED HERE: a blanket /1000 on livestock would be WRONG, because DCOW is already correct. The fix requires knowing which animal activities are on which basis, and those same yields feed the feed module (validated within ~5% of CAPRI's own reference) and the carbon MACC (validated against EcAMPA at EUR50/t). A hasty correction risks breaking two externally validated results to fix a reporting field. _reconcile_animal_yield_units in loaders.py already handles part of this and is where the work belongs. PRACTICAL WARNING, and it should be read before using the field: gross_output is SAFE for crops and for dairy, and WRONG by a factor of 1000 for pigs, poultry, calves and heifers. Do not sum it across crops and livestock. Activity levels, gross margin, nutrient balances and the market results are unaffected - this is confined to the gross_output reporting Series.
gross_output_unit_inconsistency.correction: CORRECTION to my own earlier diagnosis. I described the livestock side as 'a factor of 1000 out' with dairy correct and the rest on a kg basis. Measured properly against real EU production totals, that is wrong - the discrepancy is HETEROGENEOUS, not a uniform scaling. Computing sum(animal_numbers x yield) per activity and comparing to real EU output: DCOW gives 142,487 against a real ~155,000 kt of milk, so it is already correct as-is. But LAYS gives 1,297,711,079 against ~6,500 kt of eggs (a factor of roughly 200,000), BROI 378,570,226 against ~13,500 (28,000x), CALV 19,178,509 against ~700 (27,000x), SHGP 3,490,486 against ~600, HFRS 3,643,682 against ~2,000 and BCOW 4,271,303 against ~1,500. After dividing by 1000 the residual ratios are still 200x, 28x, 27x, 6x, 1.8x and 2.8x respectively - all different. SO THE YIELDS ARE NOT SIMPLY MIS-SCALED. Different animal activities appear to measure different THINGS: LAYS may be eggs in pieces rather than mass, BROI may be liveweight rather than carcass, CALV may be head rather than tonnes. Establishing which requires checking each against CAPRI's own output definitions, not applying a correction factor. NOT FIXED, and a scaling fix would be actively harmful: it would make the numbers LOOK right while still measuring the wrong quantity, and it would silently alter the feed module (validated within ~5% of CAPRI's reference) and the carbon MACC (validated against EcAMPA), both of which consume these yields. A wrong number that looks wrong is safer than a wrong number that looks right. THE WARNING IN THE README IS THEREFORE STRENGTHENED rather than resolved: gross_output is reliable for CROPS and for DAIRY, and should not be used for other livestock at all - not merely rescaled.
gross_output_unit_inconsistency.resolution: FIXED, after initially settling for a documented warning. The warning was the wrong call: anyone summing gross_output today got 3.9 BILLION tonnes of pig output from one NUTS-2 region, and a README caveat does not stop that reaching a briefing. A live hazard needs a code fix, not a note. THE FIX: activities whose output UNIT could not be verified now return NaN. Verification was empirical - sum(level x yield) across the EU against real output. DCOW passes (142,000 kt against a real ~155,000) and is reported. BULL, LAYS, BROI, CALV, SHGP, HFRS, BCOW, PIGS and OANI fail by factors no single rescaling explains and are suppressed. WHY NaN RATHER THAN A CORRECTION: the residual ratios after a 1000-fold adjustment are 200x, 28x, 27x, 6x, 2.8x and 1.8x - all different, so these activities measure DIFFERENT QUANTITIES (eggs possibly in pieces rather than mass, poultry liveweight rather than carcass), not the same quantity at a different scale. A rescaling would make them look plausible while the quantity remained unidentified, and would silently alter the feed module and carbon MACC, both externally validated. NaN makes a per-activity read VISIBLY unknown and makes .sum() return the verified subset. EFFECT: DE11 gross_output .sum() now gives 9,147 kt of real output instead of billions. Crops and dairy report normally (SUGB 3,485, MAIF 1,939, GRAS 908, DCOW 793). 38/38 batch-1 tests and 8/8 anchors unaffected. Pinned by test_gross_output_reports_only_verified_units. THE PRINCIPLE, worth carrying: when a quantity cannot be verified, refusing to report it beats reporting it wrongly, and beats a documentation caveat. Silence is safer than confident error.
gross_output_unit_inconsistency.root_cause_established: ROOT CAUSE ESTABLISHED from CAPRI's own data, and it is CONCEPTUAL, not a scaling error. The annex code lists define the herd activities as STOCK, not products: CALV is 'Other cows' / suckler cows (not veal, which I had wrongly compared it against), PIGS is 'Total pigs (total)', a head count. And in CAPRI's capreg DATA2 for Spain, each livestock activity carries BOTH a YILD field and separate PRODUCT items - and for breeding and suckler activities these differ: PIGF (fattening pigs) YILD 85.85 = PORK 85.85, consistent; HENS YILD 15,740 = EGGS 15,740, consistent; but SOWS YILD 19,917 against PORK 50.6, SCOW (suckler cows) YILD 422.6 against BEEF 21.8, and SHGM YILD 75.2 against SGMT 4.0. SO: CAPRI's YILD for a breeding or suckler activity measures something other than its marketed output - offspring produced, or liveweight - and the marketed product lives in its own item (PORK, BEEF, EGGS, SGMT, MILK). This model uses YILD as though it were the product. That is why no single rescaling reconciled the activities: the numbers were never the same quantity at different scales, which is what the earlier 200x / 28x / 27x residuals were showing. THIS VINDICATES THE NaN TREATMENT for a better reason than 'units unverified': for those activities, level x YILD is not a tonnage of anything saleable, so there is no correct number to report from YILD alone. THE REAL FIX is to build livestock gross output from the PRODUCT coefficients (PORK, BEEF, EGGS, SGMT, MILK per head) rather than YILD. Those coefficients exist in capreg DATA2, but are currently extracted only for ES and IT, not all 248 regions. Completing it needs the same extraction across the remaining member states - the same capreg dump the user has already produced twice.
gross_output_unit_inconsistency.final_fix: Livestock gross_output is now real marketed product. Built by tools/build_livestock_output_coef.py from capreg DATA2 dumps for all 27 member states plus Norway (user-supplied, 25 files plus ES and IT), stored at capri_data/2017/supply/livestock_output_coef.csv (kt per model head-count unit), loaded into RegionData.livestock_output_coef and used in the solve in place of YILD. METHOD: sum CAPRI's FINAL-PRODUCT items (COMI, BEEF, PORK, POUM, EGGS, SGMT, SGMI) over its ELEMENTARY livestock activities, map them onto this model's activities, and divide by the model's own regional head count, so level x coefficient reproduces CAPRI's regional output at base and scales with the model's herd in scenarios. Young-animal items are excluded (intermediate, would double-count). Countries with only a national row, and national totals not placed on a mapped region, are spread over the remaining regions by head-count share. VALIDATED: CAPRI's EU27 totals from the elementary set match real 2017 EU production - milk 0.95, beef 0.94, pork 1.01, poultry meat 0.98, eggs 1.08, sheep and goat meat 1.01. The model's EU livestock output totals 192,332 kt against CAPRI's ~201,000; the ~8,600 kt gap is Ireland, which has no herds in this model (see ireland_livestock_missing). A full EU base run reproduces the build to within 0.14%. DE11 now reports 163 kt of pork, where it once reported 3.9 billion tonnes. FIVE TRAPS HIT DURING THE BUILD, recorded because each is a trap for the next person: (1) aggregate rows (UAAR, CATA, RUMI, AGGT) and the expenditure row EXPD carry product items too, and summing them gave totals thousands of times too high; (2) DCOL/DCOH and BULH are intensity VARIANTS of DCOW and BULF, and including them doubled milk; (3) GAMS writes Eps for tiny values and a numeric pattern matched its leading E; (4) MY OWN region pattern accepted only digits after the country code and silently dropped every letter-coded region - a third of Germany's milk and nearly all of France's - the same silent-drop family this project keeps finding, reintroduced in new code; (5) the new CSV was not registered in loaders._FILE_CATEGORY, so it resolved to a non-existent path and every livestock value came back NaN. NOT FIXED: gross_margin. Livestock net revenue still uses price x YILD, so the margin remains dominated by quantities that are not marketed products. Fixing it changes the PMP linear term and therefore calibration, and was deliberately left for a separate, verified change.

capri_official_documentation.status: located; activity set validated against it
capri_official_documentation.note: The user supplied the official CAPRI documentation at https://bw-pages.thuenen.de/capri/capri/ (Thuenen Institute, VuePress). It was not previously known to this project and is authoritative for several things previously INFERRED from the GAMS source. CONFIRMS THE DATA PIPELINE we had reconstructed: raw sources (Eurostat, FAOSTAT, OECD, FADN) -> COCO 'the Complete and Consistent Data Base' at NATIONAL scale -> CAPREG, the regionalised database -> input allocation -> global components and policy data. The stated purpose matches what reconcile_base.py was built to do: 'Specific modules ensure that the data used in CAPRI are mutually compatible and complete in time and space.' So our reconciliation is reproducing COCO's job, and the concordance gap we hit is exactly the Eurostat->activity mapping COCO performs. ACTIVITY SET VALIDATED against the documented code lists (annex_code_lists). Our 29 crop activities are a SUBSET of CAPRI's with two renames and one aggregation, all now confirmed rather than guessed: MAIZ (CAPRI) = CORN (ours), which is the alias behind the grain-maize bug; TWIN (CAPRI) = WINE (ours); TEXT (CAPRI) is split into COTT + OFIB here. CAPRI's documented groups also place OLIV inside OILS with RAPE/SOYA/SUNF/PARI, and FRU = {APPL, CITR, TAGR, TWIN}. A GENUINE OMISSION FOUND: PARI (paddy rice) is in CAPRI's OILS group and is ABSENT from this model entirely - not under PARI, not under RICE, and not folded into OCER (which totals 3,310 kha against a real EU rice area of roughly 400 kha, mostly Italy ~220 and Spain ~100). EU rice is small but not negligible and is concentrated in two member states, so regional results for Lombardy, Piedmont and the Ebro delta are missing an activity that matters locally. ALSO SETTLED - trade region count: I had flagged a concern that our 29 trade regions might under-represent CAPRI's '40 trade regions'. The Thuenen model page states 28 trade blocks, so 29 is right and the concern was unfounded. AND CONFIRMS OUR FRAMING: the documentation states plainly that CAPRI 'is a comparative static model', with recursive-dynamic capability added later by CAPRI-Dynaspat. Our description of the core as comparative-static with a projection layer on top is correct. STILL TO READ, and both are directly useful: the 'The CAPRI Data Base' chapter would let us validate reconcile_base.py against CAPRI's documented method rather than against GAMS inference, and the full code-list annex is the concordance source I had earlier said did not exist in accessible form.

capri_documentation_read.status: method and several inferences confirmed; two gaps quantified
capri_documentation_read.note: Read the official CAPRI Modelling System Documentation (Britz ed., 2005, 133pp, capri-model.org). It confirms several things this project had INFERRED from GAMS source, corrects nothing material, and quantifies two gaps. 1. OUR RECONCILIATION METHOD IS THE ONE CAPRI USES. Section 2.3.2 describes COCO as 'minimisation of normalised least squares under constraints' with accounting identities as constraints and engineering bounds - and explicitly records that the team CHOSE modified least squares over Cross or Maximum Entropy estimators ('the ex-ante knowledge can be expressed mainly relating to the estimated value and not in relation to estimated parameters'). reconcile_base.py independently arrived at weighted least squares for the same reason. That is a strong methodological validation, not a coincidence. 2. THE CONCORDANCE IS DOCUMENTED, and my inference about the archive file was CORRECT. Section 2.4.8: 'Only some few crop activities are available in REGIO (cereals with wheat, barley, grain maize, rice; potatoes, sugar beet, oil seeds with rape and sunflower; tobacco, fodder maize; grassland, permanent crops with vineyards and olive plantations). The COCO data base, however, covers some 30 different crop activities. In order to break these aggregates down to COCO definitions, THE NATIONAL SHARES OF THE AGGREGATE ARE USED.' That is exactly what base_areas_eurostat.csv is, and it explains the 35% repeating decimals found there. The earlier correction to the 32% claim was right. 3. PERFECT AGGREGATION matches our approach too. Section 2.4.9 applies correction factors CORR = national_level / sum(regional_levels), then Levl = Levl* x CORR - proportional scaling, which is what _project_to_total does. 4. A DIRECT CHECK ON OUR ASSUMED PESTICIDE COST. Table 1 of the documentation gives a real CAPRI activity record (Denmark soft wheat, 2000-2002): PLAP 59.85 EUR/ha against TOIN 522.13 EUR/ha, an 11.5% share. Our PPP_COST_SHARE for SWHE is 5.7% (40.0 EUR/ha on a variable cost of 702). CAPRI's documented share is 2.0x ours. That does not automatically mean ours is wrong - different country, period and price base, and our share is derived from ES and IT PESTOTAL quantities rather than Denmark - but it is the first external reference point on this quantity and it suggests our pesticide cost channel may be UNDERSTATED by roughly half, which would push the Farm-to-Fork cereal result further from CAPRI's, not closer. 5. TWO PRODUCTION INTENSITIES. CAPRI splits dairy cows, bull fattening and heifer fattening into low/high variants (DCOL/DCOH at 60%/140% of average milk yield, BULL/BULH and HEIL/HEIH at +/-20% meat output) specifically to avoid overstating technological rigidity. This model has no such split - a documented structural simplification not previously recorded. 6. TRADE BLOCKS: the 2005 documentation says 18 trading blocks over ~40 countries; the current Thuenen page says 28. Our 29 is consistent with the current figure.

capri_regio_concordance.nature: DATA_ACQUIRED — closes a gap previously called inaccessible
capri_regio_concordance.note: The CAPRI-REGIO concordance is PUBLIC and now in the repo at capri_data/shared/capri_regio_concordance.json. Source: CAPRI Online Manual, Annex: Code lists, Tables 1-4 (capri-model.org, last modified 2022-11-07, CC0 1.0). Table 3 is CAPRI's own 'Connection between CAPRI and REGIO crop areas, crop production and herd sizes'. THIS CORRECTS AN EARLIER STATEMENT OF MINE. I had recorded that a real concordance 'cannot be built from this repo' and that the mapping was not available in accessible form, so that deriving it from the numbers would be circular. The first half was right - it is not in the repo - but the conclusion was wrong: it is published, freely licensed, and took one fetch. I had not looked. WHAT IT CONTAINS: 34 crop mappings from REGIO collection categories to CAPRI activities, plus the animal mappings. It also confirms the share-allocation mechanism documented in section 2.4.8 - REGIO carries only a few aggregates and CAPRI breaks them down using NATIONAL SHARES - which is the direct explanation for the 35% repeating decimals found in base_areas_eurostat.csv. That file is share-allocated by construction, exactly as inferred. TEN ACTIVITIES CAPRI CARRIES AND THIS MODEL DOES NOT, now enumerated against the authoritative Annex Table 4 rather than guessed: PARI (paddy rice), OIND (other industrial crops), TABO (table olives, distinct from OLIV olives-for-oil), OWIN (other wine, distinct from TWIN table wine), NURS (nursery plants), FLOW (flowers and ornamentals), OCRO (other marketable crops), ROOF (fodder root crops), NONF (non-food on set-aside), FALL (fallow, folded into SETA here). AND THREE ALIASES CONFIRMED: our CORN = CAPRI MAIZ, our WINE = CAPRI TWIN, our COTT+OFIB is a different split of CAPRI's TEXT. WHAT THIS UNBLOCKS: a Eurostat-based base year is no longer blocked on an unavailable mapping. The remaining work is applying this concordance to raw REGIO extracts and validating the result against CAPRI's reconciled base - which reconcile_base.py can now do, since its method is confirmed to be the one COCO uses.

capri_2022_documentation.status: current version obtained; CAPTRD chapter read
capri_2022_documentation.note: The user supplied caprijan2022.pdf - the CURRENT CAPRI documentation, 348 pages, January 2022. This supersedes the 2005 PDF read earlier and removes the twenty-year staleness caveat that was attached to those findings. Chapter map recorded in CAPRI_REFERENCE.md: data base p23, baseline generation p145, scenario simulation p178, post model analysis p283, CAPDIS p303, code lists p338. CHAPTER 4 (BASELINE GENERATION / CAPTRD) READ - the counterpart to this model's projection layer. THE MOST USEFUL FINDING is CAPRI's own assessment of its baseline process: 'baselines are in most cases not a straight outcome from a model but developed using a combination of trend analysis, model runs and expert consultations... IT IS ALMOST UNAVOIDABLE THAT THE PROCESS IS SOMEWHAT INTRANSPARENT.' That is a direct endorsement of this project's decision to treat the trajectory as an exogenous, versioned, swappable input rather than generating it internally, and it is now quoted in the README where that design choice is explained. It also means a reimplementation CANNOT fully reproduce a CAPRI baseline, because part of it is expert judgement rather than algorithm - a boundary worth knowing. CAPTRD'S THREE STEPS map onto our trajectory/reconcile split: (1) independent trends with goodness-of-fit statistics, (2) impose identities and technical bounds, (3) add 'supports' from external results (AgLink, Commission projections) and break down from Member State to regional level. The trend estimates are explicitly a 'SAFETY NET' where no external projection exists - the same role our per-activity medians play where regional detail is missing. AND AN INDEPENDENT ARRIVAL AT THE SAME CHECK: CAPRI's baseline workflow ends with a 'no change' simulation whose stated purpose is 'to verify that the calibration of the baseline worked as intended'. That is conceptually our null-trajectory identity test. Two teams reaching the same verification design is reassuring about it.
capri_2022_documentation.chapter5: CHAPTER 5 (SCENARIO SIMULATION / CAPMOD) READ. Two findings change what we know about our own results. 1. THE PERMANENT-CROP ELASTICITY STRUCTURE IS DELIBERATE, and now explained structurally rather than just measured. The PMP first-order condition is Rev_j = Cost_j + ac_j + sum_k bc_jk Levl_k + sum_i lambda_i a_ij, and the documentation states: 'The cross effects are only introduced to let major arable crop groups interact, whereas for FRUITS & VEGETABLES, PERMANENT CROPS, GRASSLAND AND THE ANIMAL SECTORS, ONLY DIAGONAL TERMS ARE INTRODUCED.' So CAPRI gives permanents no cross-price substitution by design. That independently confirms the 0.18-0.22 values we extracted from supply_elas_*.gdx, and shows my earlier rescaling of permanents UPWARD was wrong for a structural reason and not merely an empirical one. 2. CAPRI HAS A GENERAL INTENSITY MARGIN, wider than ours. Stage one of its two-stage process chooses variable input coefficients per ha/head for given yields, where yields are 'determined exogenously by trend analysis (CAPRI reference scenario) AND UPDATED DEPENDING ON PRICE CHANGES AGAINST THE BASELINE'. Our supply/intensity.py implements the nitrogen part of that only - the yield response to price is absent here. A documented structural gap not previously recorded. 3. MARKET MODULE FORM confirmed: normalised quadratic for feed, processing and supply; generalised Leontief expenditure for human consumption; homogeneity of degree zero, symmetry and correct curvature imposed; Armington bilateral trade; dairy with fat and protein balancing equations. The iteration loop matches ours - supply at exogenous prices, aggregate, young-animal trade module, market calibrated to supply results then solved, producer prices back to supply, premiums adjusted between iterations if CMO ceilings overshoot. 4. AN UNRESOLVED DISCREPANCY: chapter 5 says the market module covers '40 country aggregates or trading partners', while the current Thuenen model page says 28 trade blocks and this model has 29. Which figure is current is unclear. Worth settling before claiming our world coverage is complete - I previously recorded the 28 figure as settling this, which was premature.

pmp_cross_terms_permanents.status: real, tested, and NOT cheaply fixable
pmp_cross_terms_permanents.note: CAPRI's documentation (chapter 5) states that PMP cross-price terms are introduced 'only to let major arable crop groups interact, whereas for fruits & vegetables, permanent crops, grassland and the animal sectors, only diagonal terms are introduced'. CHECKED AGAINST OURS: our Q matrix has ALL 312 permanent-crop off-diagonal entries non-zero for ES61, where CAPRI has zero. A genuine structural divergence, not a parameter difference. TESTED THE OBVIOUS FIX AND IT FAILS. Zeroing the permanent-crop cross terms post-calibration collapses base fidelity from 0.61% to 50.54%. The reason is straightforward in hindsight: the Q matrix is CALIBRATED WITH those terms present, so removing them afterwards destroys the calibration that makes the base year reproduce. A correct fix would impose the diagonal-only structure DURING PMP calibration, which changes the calibration procedure rather than patching its output. AND THE BENEFIT IS UNCERTAIN, which is why this is recorded rather than done. Our realized permanent-crop own-price elasticities ALREADY match CAPRI's calibrated values exactly (APPL 0.218 vs 0.218, CITR 0.184 vs 0.184, OVEG 0.660 vs 0.663). So the cross terms are not distorting the own-price response, which is the quantity we can check. What they WOULD distort is cross-price substitution between permanents and arable crops - a channel CAPRI deliberately closes and we cannot currently validate, because no CAPRI cross-price reference for permanents is in hand. SO: a documented divergence with a known cause, a failed cheap fix, and an uncertain payoff. Worth doing only alongside a re-derivation of the PMP calibration, and only if a cross-price reference becomes available to check the result against. Imposing it blind would trade a measured-correct own-price response for an unmeasurable cross-price one.

yield_price_response.status: implemented and validated; closes a gap found by reading CAPRI ch.5
yield_price_response.note: CAPRI's supply model uses a TWO-STAGE decision process (documentation ch. 5): stage one sets variable input coefficients per hectare for given yields, where those yields are 'determined exogenously by trend analysis (CAPRI reference scenario) AND UPDATED DEPENDING ON PRICE CHANGES AGAINST THE BASELINE'; stage two solves the activity mix. This model had no such yield response - a price shock moved AREA only, a pure extensive margin, which understates supply response and overstates the area change needed to deliver it. The same class of gap as the nitrogen intensity margin, found the same way: by reading what CAPRI documents rather than inferring from output. IMPLEMENTED as SupplyModel.apply_yield_price_response: yield_new = yield_base * (1 + dp) ** eps, applied to own-price changes, with net revenue rebuilt from the adjusted yields so the price effect enters once through quantity and once through yield - which is what a two-stage decision implies. Called after _compute_net_revenues so it is not overwritten by the rebuild. THE ASSUMPTION, exposed as YIELD_PRICE_ELASTICITY = 0.15 rather than buried: a short-run own-price yield elasticity from the agronomic and econometric literature (typically 0.1-0.3 - intensification through fertiliser, protection and management responds within a season, variety and structure do not). NOT tuned to any comparison. THE IDENTITY THAT MAKES IT SAFE: at an unchanged price the factor is exactly 1.0, so the base year is reproduced bit-for-bit and PMP calibration is untouched. Verified: base fidelity 0.47% UNCHANGED, 248/248 regions still converge, 8/8 regression anchors green, 37/37 batch-1 tests pass. A LEAK CAUGHT DURING IMPLEMENTATION: the method rewrites data.yields, which was not in the solve's backup/restore block - the adjusted yields would have leaked into every subsequent solve on the same model. Exactly the failure the nutrient_coefs snapshot was added to prevent, recurring because the block lists what to restore rather than restoring everything mutable. Added. EFFECT: a 10% wheat price rise on FR10 now gives +1.44% yield alongside +5.28% area, where before the entire response was area. Pinned by test_yield_responds_to_price, which checks both the zero-shock identity and that the elasticity stays in a plausible short-run range.

solve_state_leaks_fixed.note: The solve's restore block ENUMERATED which fields to restore, and that list fell behind TWICE: nutrient_coefs leaked until the nitrogen intensity margin was traced, and yields leaked again the moment the yield-price response was added. Each leak is silent - an altered value simply persists into every later solve on the same model, so results depend on what was run before them. The second occurrence is the point. Enumerating what to restore puts the burden on whoever adds the NEXT mutation to remember a block elsewhere in the file, and that burden was not met either time.
